reason: Encryption page: both encrypted and unencrypted volumes can be attached to an instance simultaneously; examples page: with access to both, you can freely transfer data between them.
What-is-EBS features list states encryption runs on the EC2 host servers and secures data at rest and in transit between instance, attached volume and subsequent snapshots.
Snapshots section states both halves verbatim: snapshots of encrypted volumes and volumes from encrypted snapshots are automatically encrypted.
Supported volume types section: same IOPS as unencrypted, minimal effect on latency, encryption and decryption transparent with no action from you or applications.
Permissions for users: users must be granted the listed KMS actions (CreateGrant, Decrypt, DescribeKey, GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext, ReEncrypt); the tip supports the least-privilege display.
Console step: after increasing size you must also extend the partition to use the added capacity; the same step links to 'Extend the file system after resizing', which covers the file-system part.
FAQ states average EC2-to-EBS latency is single-digit milliseconds and io2 Block Express average latency is sub-millisecond.
FAQ defines Block Express as next-generation EBS storage server architecture with sub-millisecond latency that uses SRD to talk to Nitro-based instances.
FAQ recommends, when a volume is detached, considering a snapshot and deleting the volume to reduce costs.
FAQ answer states GetSnapshotBlock and PutSnapshotBlock support 512KiB block size.

Two FAQ answers: encrypted data volumes at launch with AWS-managed or customer-managed keys, including volumes not in the AMI, via BlockDeviceMapping in RunInstances or the launch wizard.
FAQ: encryption by default with a single setting per region ensures all new volumes are always encrypted.
FAQ: EBS encryption covers data volumes, boot volumes and snapshots without building your own key management infrastructure.
FAQ: data at rest encrypted with Amazon-managed keys or keys you create and manage in KMS.
FAQ (encryption key management): each new volume gets a unique 256-bit AES key; volumes from the encrypted snapshots share the key.

The same FAQ elsewhere says FSR cannot be applied to shared snapshots, but the EBS user guide FSR page confirms shared snapshots are supported, so that older FAQ line is stale.
